Does my job qualify for "no tax on tips"?

The tip cap and the MAGI phase-out are the arithmetic the calculator below does for you. Whether your occupation qualifies at all is a different question, and it's the one the calculator can't answer -- it only asks you to confirm it. This page covers what's actually on Treasury's final list, the cutoff date that trips people up, and what does and doesn't count as a "tip" in the first place.

Open the free calculator

The 8 categories on Treasury's final list

Treasury and the IRS published final regulations on April 13, 2026 (effective June 12, 2026) listing 71 occupations across 8 categories -- more than 200 example job titles in all -- that "customarily and regularly" receive tips. The final list grew from 68 occupations in the September 2025 proposed rule after a public comment period and an October 2025 hearing.

CategoryExample occupations
Beverage and Food ServiceBartenders, wait staff, dishwashers, baristas, food servers
Entertainment and EventsMusicians, DJs, performers, event staff
Hospitality and Guest ServicesConcierges, housekeeping staff, bellhops, hotel front desk
Home ServicesRepair workers, groundskeepers, movers who work directly in the home
Personal ServicesEvent planners, photographers, personal care aides
Personal Appearance and WellnessHair and makeup stylists, barbers, nail technicians, personal trainers
Recreation and InstructionTour guides, activity instructors, golf caddies
Transportation and DeliveryTaxi and rideshare drivers, movers, delivery workers

This table is illustrative, not the full list. Before filing, check your specific job title against Treasury's published occupation list and the Treasury Tipped Occupation Code (TTOC) your employer reports.

The rule that actually decides most edge cases: the December 31, 2024 cutoff

My job isn't on the list but customers do tip me -- do I qualify?

No, not on tips from that job. Eligibility is not about whether you personally received a tip; it is about whether your occupation customarily and regularly received tips on or before December 31, 2024. A role that only recently started getting tipped, or one that received tips occasionally rather than customarily, does not newly qualify just because a customer left one.

That cutoff is the detail a quick "is my job on the list" search usually misses, because it reads like an occupation test alone. It's actually an occupation-as-practiced-before-2025 test: the question isn't "could someone in this job receive a tip," it's "did this occupation, as a whole, already have a customary practice of tipping before the law existed." Treasury built the list from 2023 tax data, Department of Labor caselaw, and survey data specifically to answer that backward-looking question, not a forward-looking one.

What counts as a "tip" -- and what doesn't

Does an automatic 18% gratuity on a large party count as a qualified tip?

No. A mandatory service charge or automatic gratuity is not a tip under the final regulations, even when the employer later distributes it to the worker -- it is treated as wages, not a customer-given tip. If a customer voluntarily adds an extra amount on top of that mandatory charge, that additional voluntary portion can qualify.

The line the regulations actually draw is who decides the amount. A tip has to be voluntary, with the customer choosing whether to pay it and how much -- paid in cash or a cash-equivalent (check, credit or debit card, gift card, an app that transfers cash value), whether handed over directly or split through a legitimate tip pool. A charge the business sets and adds automatically, however it's later distributed, isn't one. A handheld point-of-sale prompt that offers 15%, 18%, 20%, another amount, or no tip produces a qualified tip either way, because the customer genuinely had the option to leave nothing; a bill that simply adds 18% for parties of six or more does not, because the customer never had that choice.

Worked example: how much the occupation question is actually worth

How much difference does the occupation question actually make?

For $18,000 of qualified tips at a 22% marginal rate and MAGI under the phase-out threshold, the calculator below shows an $18,000 deduction and about $3,960 of estimated federal tax savings if the occupation qualifies -- and $0 of either if it doesn't. The whole deduction turns on that one checkbox.

Occupation eligibilityDeductionEstimated savings at 22%
On Treasury's list$18,000$3,960
Not on the list (or unconfirmed)$0$0

Nothing else about the return changes between those two rows -- same tips, same MAGI, same marginal rate. Confirming occupation eligibility against the actual published list, rather than guessing, is worth doing before you rely on the larger number.

Common questions

How many occupations are on Treasury's tip occupation list?

71 occupations across 8 categories, covering more than 200 example job titles, in the final regulations Treasury and the IRS published on April 13, 2026 (effective June 12, 2026). The list expanded from 68 proposed occupations after a public comment period and an October 2025 hearing.

How will my qualifying tips show up on my W-2?

Starting with tax year 2026, employers report qualified cash tips under code "TP" in Box 12 and your Treasury Tipped Occupation Code (TTOC) in the new Box 14b. For tax year 2025 returns, most filers estimate qualified tips from pay records instead, since the new box didn't exist yet.

What's the "no tax on tips" and "no tax on overtime" deduction worth?

Two new federal deductions apply to tax years 2025 through 2028: up to $25,000 of qualified tips, and up to $12,500 ($25,000 married filing jointly) of qualified overtime compensation — but only the half-time premium portion of overtime pay, not your full time-and-a-half wages, and both shrink once your income clears $150,000 (single) or $300,000 (joint). This estimates both, including the part people usually get wrong.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

1. Filing status & income

MAGI here is modified adjusted gross income — for most filers with no foreign income or certain exclusions, this is close to the AGI on last year's return, adjusted for this year's income. Not sure of your bracket? See the reference table below the results.

2. Qualified tips

Schedule 1-A's instructions (clarified 2026-03) cap the deduction at this net profit minus deductions allocable to the business -- not raw net profit. If you claim any of these against this business, enter the amounts below so the ceiling is accurate. Leave blank if none apply.

3. Qualified overtime compensation

This is only the extra half-time premium on overtime hours — not your full overtime pay. If you already know the figure (for example, tax year 2025+ W-2s show it in Box 14 as "FLSA OT Prem"), enter it directly. Otherwise compute it from your hours below.

Add a row per hourly rate you were paid overtime at this year: rate, overtime hours in a typical week at that rate, and how many weeks. Premium = rate × 0.5 × overtime hours × weeks. Worked at two different rates in the same week? Use this portfolio's own blended-rate overtime calculator first and enter its overtime-premium-per-hour figure as the rate here — that FLSA weighted-average arithmetic is already built and tested there.

Common questions

How much can I deduct under 'no tax on tips'?

Up to $25,000 of qualified cash tips per year, for tax years 2025 through 2028, if your occupation is on Treasury's published list of occupations that customarily and regularly receive tips. The deduction phases out for higher earners -- see the phase-out question below.

How much can I deduct under 'no tax on overtime'?

Up to $12,500 per year (single or head of household) or $25,000 (married filing jointly) of qualified overtime compensation, for tax years 2025 through 2028 -- but only the FLSA 'half-time' premium portion of overtime pay (the extra 0.5x for hours over 40 in a week), not your full time-and-a-half overtime wages. If you earned $30/hr on overtime hours from a $20/hr regular rate, only the $10/hr premium counts, not the full $30/hr.

What is the income phase-out for these deductions?

Both deductions are reduced by $100 for every $1,000 (or part of $1,000) that your modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) exceeds $150,000 (single or head of household) or $300,000 (married filing jointly). The tip deduction reaches $0 at $400,000 MAGI single / $550,000 joint. The overtime deduction reaches $0 at $275,000 MAGI single or head of household (its cap is smaller) / $550,000 joint.

Do these deductions reduce Social Security, Medicare, or state income tax?

No. Both are federal income-tax deductions only. Your tips and overtime pay remain fully subject to Social Security and Medicare (FICA) tax if you are an employee, or self-employment (SECA) tax if you are self-employed, and most states will still tax them in full unless that state has separately chosen to conform to the federal deduction.

Can I claim these if I file married filing separately?

No. Both deductions require married taxpayers to file a joint return; married filing separately is not eligible for either one.

Is this tax advice?

No. This calculator applies the published statutory caps and phase-out formula to the numbers you enter. It is not a full tax return, it does not know your complete tax situation, and it is not a substitute for reviewing the IRS's own guidance or consulting a qualified tax professional before you file.

vs-estimating-the-deduction-by-hand.html.text:

This calculator vs. doing it by hand

The "no tax on tips" and "no tax on overtime" deductions are arithmetic anyone can do with a calculator or worksheet. The problem is that each has a non-obvious step that a quick by-hand estimate tends to skip — the overtime deduction is only half the overtime rate, and the phase-out rounds up, not down.

Where a hand estimate usually goes wrong

StepCommon mistake by handWhat this calculator does
Overtime deduction amountUses the full time-and-a-half overtime pay ($30/hr example) instead of just the extra half-time premium ($10/hr), overstating the deduction roughly 3x.Computes rate × 0.5 × overtime hours × weeks — the premium-only figure the statute actually allows.
The MAGI phase-outSkipped entirely, or the excess over the threshold is rounded down to the nearest $1,000 instead of up.Reduces each deduction by $100 per $1,000 of MAGI over the threshold, rounding the excess UP ("or fraction thereof") — $150,001 costs the same first $100 as $150,999.
Adding tips and overtime togetherAdds gross tips and gross overtime pay into one uncapped total.Caps each deduction separately ($25,000 tips; $12,500/$25,000 overtime) and phases each out independently before summing.
Self-employed tip incomeDeducts the full qualified-tips figure even when net profit from that specific tipped work is lower.Caps the self-employed tip deduction at net profit from the tipped trade or business, when that figure is entered.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Common questions

What's the most common mistake estimating the overtime deduction by hand?

Using the full time-and-a-half overtime rate instead of only the half-time premium. Qualified overtime compensation is just the extra 0.5x portion of the overtime rate over the regular rate -- someone earning $30/hr on overtime from a $20/hr base has $10/hr of qualified premium, not $30/hr. Using the full rate overstates the deduction by 3x.

What's the most common mistake with the income phase-out?

Forgetting it applies at all, or rounding the excess MAGI down to the nearest $1,000 instead of up. The statute reduces the deduction by $100 per $1,000 of MAGI over the threshold, 'or fraction thereof' -- so $150,001 of MAGI already costs the first $100, the same as $150,999 does. Rounding down understates the phase-out and overstates the deduction near a $1,000 boundary.

Can I just add up my full overtime pay and my tips and call it the deduction?

No. Tips are capped at $25,000 and overtime premium is capped separately at $12,500 (single/head of household) or $25,000 (joint) -- and both totals shrink independently once MAGI clears $150,000 single or $300,000 joint. Adding uncapped totals together overstates the deduction for anyone near or above either cap or threshold.

Does a self-employed tip earner get the full amount regardless of profit?

No. For self-employment income, the deduction cannot exceed net profit from the specific tipped trade or business, even if qualified tips received and the phased-out cap would otherwise allow more -- a common omission in a quick by-hand estimate that only looks at gross tips.

Does this calculator know my complete tax situation?

No. Neither this calculator nor a by-hand worksheet built from this page knows your full return -- other deductions, credits, self-employment tax, or state conformity. Both apply the same published federal caps and phase-out formula to the numbers you enter; verify against the IRS's own guidance or a qualified tax professional before filing.
